A $13\,\text{ft}$ support pole leans against a vertical wall, forming an angle $\theta $ with the ground. The base of the pole $B$ is being pulled toward the wall at a rate of $2\,\text{ft/s}.$ At what rate is $\theta $ increasing at the moment when the top of the pole $T$ is $5\,\text{ft}$ above the ground? Do not round the answer.

The angle is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$

current_example.problem:
Peter is standing on the bank of a river. He observes a speed boat $B$ going downstream at a constant distance of $10\,\textrm{m}$ from the bank. If the boat moves at a constant speed of $8 \, \textrm{m/s}$ parallel to the bank, at what rate is the angle $\theta,$ between the observer's line of sight to the boat and the bank, decreasing when $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}6?$ Assume the angle of elevation is decreasing at a **positive** rate, and do not round the answer.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/abf063d149ae14c11b9ca62208a4390b32ae191418c2e0fe77f6038479fd5625.png)
current_example.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/113109cb44fd2d10cd3b88324ed58d2ff6455a25c81b4f62eb1862b7ced03b52.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the distance between the boat and the bank and $x$ is the horizontal distance traveled by that boat after passing Peter. The quantity $y=10$ meters does not change with time because the boat is at a constant distance from the bank.

We wish to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\theta}{\textrm{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{10}{x} \\ x & =10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-10{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=8$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}6.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =(-10{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}))\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & ={(2)}^{2}\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & =4\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate at which the angle $\theta$ is decreasing is $\dfrac{1}{5}$ radians per second.
